# Part 1: Set Up Your Reproducible Workflow

**Purpose:** Reproduce, extend, and explain descriptive statistics on student
performance in the COSC 423 one-group results file.

**How to run this document**

1. Put `Lab_1_Results_Analysis.Rmd` and `COSC_423_Results_for_One_Group.xlsx`
   in the *same folder* (an RStudio Project is ideal, so the folder is the
   working directory).
2. Install any missing packages once, from the Console (not inside this file):
   `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "readxl", "rmarkdown"))`
3. Click **Knit** (or run `rmarkdown::render("Lab_1_Results_Analysis.Rmd")`).

Good reproducibility means anyone reading your code can run it and get
identical results. Always load packages, set seeds, and document your purpose
at the top.

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)   # includes ggplot2, dplyr, readr
library(readxl)

set.seed(42)         # no random numbers are used below, but we set it anyway
```

## Load the dataset

The sheet is laid out like a gradebook rather than a tidy table:

* rows 1–2 hold section titles and mark weights,
* row 3 holds the column headers, and
* the headers repeat (`Total` appears twice and `Exam` appears twice) and the
  20 attendance headers are dates.

Reading it with default settings therefore gives awkward names, and there is
**no column called `total_score`** (this is what caused the
`Unknown or uninitialised column` warning). Instead, we read the data
starting at row 4 and assign clear names ourselves. The final overall mark
(out of 100) is the second `Total` column, column AS in Excel.

```{r load}
col_names <- c(
  "class_id",
  sprintf("att_s%02d", 1:20),                       # B:U  attendance, 20 sessions (0/1)
  "att_total", "att_marks", "att_pct",              # V:X  sessions attended, /5 marks, %
  "gender", "cgpa_range",                           # Y:Z
  "att_score",                                      # AA   attendance mark (/5)
  "q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5", "q6", "quiz",       # AB:AH
  "a1", "a2", "ass",                                # AI:AK assignments
  "mid_sem",                                        # AL
  "ca",                                             # AM   continuous assessment (/40)
  "python_lab", "r_lab",                            # AN:AO
  "exam_100", "exam_30", "main_exam",               # AP:AR
  "total_score",                                    # AS   overall mark (/100)
  "grade", "pass_fail"                              # AT:AU
)

results <- read_excel(
  "COSC_423_Results_for_One_Group.xlsx",
  range     = cell_limits(c(4, 1), c(NA, length(col_names))),  # start at row 4, columns A:AU
  col_names = col_names
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(class_id))        # drop the blank rows below the last student

# Fail early (with a clear message) if the file did not load as expected
stopifnot(is.numeric(results$total_score), nrow(results) > 0)
```

## Inspect the data

```{r inspect}
head(results)
dim(results)
str(results)
sum(is.na(results$total_score))   # number of missing total scores
```

The file contains **`r nrow(results)` students** and `r ncol(results)`
variables, with no missing total scores. One data-quality note: a few
`cgpa_range` labels such as `"2.50 - 2.100"` and `"3.50 - 3.49"` look like
typos (probably mistyped or auto-corrected in Excel). They are not used in
this lab, but would need cleaning before any analysis by CGPA band.

# Part 2: Compute Descriptive Statistics

Measures of center and spread summarise the class's performance.

```{r descriptives}
# Extract total scores
scores <- results$total_score

# Measures of center
mean_score   <- mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
median_score <- median(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
mode_score   <- as.numeric(names(sort(table(scores), decreasing = TRUE)[1]))

# Measures of spread
var_score   <- var(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_score    <- sd(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
range_score <- max(scores, na.rm = TRUE) - min(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
iq_range    <- IQR(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Create a summary table
summary_stats <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean", "Median", "Mode", "Variance", "Std Dev", "Range", "IQR"),
  Value     = c(mean_score, median_score, mode_score, var_score,
                sd_score, range_score, iq_range)
)

print(summary_stats)
```

**A note on the mode.** Total scores are continuous (e.g. 46.289, 68.153), so
almost every value is unique and the "mode" above (`r mode_score`) is just
the one value shared by a handful of students who scored near zero. It says
nothing useful about the typical student. A more meaningful mode groups scores
into bands of 5 marks:

```{r modal-bin}
score_bands <- cut(scores, breaks = seq(0, 90, by = 5), right = FALSE)
table(score_bands)
names(which.max(table(score_bands)))   # modal band
```

**Interpretation.**

```{r desc-extras, include=FALSE}
skew_score <- mean((scores - mean_score)^3) / (sqrt(mean((scores - mean_score)^2)))^3
q <- unname(quantile(scores, c(0.25, 0.75)))
n_low <- sum(scores < 10)
```

The class averaged **`r round(mean_score, 2)` out of 100**, with a median of
**`r round(median_score, 2)`**. Because the mean sits about
`r round(median_score - mean_score, 1)` marks *below* the median, the
distribution is **left-skewed** (moment skewness = `r round(skew_score, 2)`): a
small group of very low scores drags the mean down. The standard deviation of
`r round(sd_score, 2)` is large (about a third of the mean), so variability is
high, and the middle 50% of students scored between `r round(q[1], 1)` and
`r round(q[2], 1)` (IQR = `r round(iq_range, 2)`). The range runs from
`r round(min(scores), 2)` to `r round(max(scores), 2)`
(`r round(range_score, 2)` marks). The modal 5-mark band is 65 to under 70, which
holds the largest group of students. `r n_low` students scored below 10; in
the data these students attended only 1 to 5 of the 20 sessions and earned
almost nothing in the exam, which is consistent with disengagement or
withdrawal. As a lecturer, I
would note that the typical student performed reasonably (median above 60), but
the low tail points to a separate engagement problem, and the cohort is far
from uniform in preparation.

# Part 3: Explore Probability Distributions

Use visualisation and reasoning to decide which distributions fit the data.

```{r histogram}
# Visualize the distribution of total scores
ggplot(results, aes(x = total_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = "steelblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_score,   color = "red",   linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median_score, color = "green4", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Scores",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = mean, green dashed line = median",
       x = "Total Score", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r qqplot}
# Assess normality with a Q-Q plot
qqnorm(scores)
qqline(scores, col = "red")
```

```{r shapiro}
# Formal normality test (Shapiro-Wilk)
shapiro_test <- shapiro.test(scores)
print(shapiro_test)
```

**Reading the plots.** The histogram peaks at 65–70 with a long tail stretching
left toward zero, and the red mean line sits to the left of the green median
line, which is the signature of left skew. In the Q-Q plot the points bend away
from the red line in the lower-left corner (the low scorers), so the
lower tail is much heavier than a normal distribution's. The Shapiro-Wilk test
agrees: W = `r round(shapiro_test$statistic, 3)`,
p = `r signif(shapiro_test$p.value, 3)`. This is far below 0.05, so we **reject
normality** for the raw scores.

**Scenario reasoning: why different scenarios fit different distributions**

* **Binomial:** A 10-question True/False quiz fits a binomial distribution
  because each question has two outcomes (pass/fail), a fixed number of trials
  (10), and a constant probability of success per question. In this dataset,
  the number of students who pass out of the `r nrow(results)` is also
  binomial-like (each student passes or fails, fixed `n`, one pass mark),
  provided students are independent: `r sum(results$pass_fail == "Pass")`
  passed.
* **Poisson:** Daily attendance counts fit a Poisson distribution if events
  (students arriving) are independent and occur at a constant average rate with
  no fixed upper limit. Here, attendance per session is capped at the class size
  and the attendance probability is high, so a *binomial* is the better model
  for this class. Poisson suits unbounded counts of rare events, such as the
  number of help-desk emails per day.
* **Normal:** Total exam scores often approximate normality due to the Central
  Limit Theorem: many factors contribute to a score, and their sum tends toward
  a bell curve. That is only an approximation, though. These scores are capped
  at 100, many students score near zero when they drop out, and the Shapiro-Wilk
  test rejects normality. The Central Limit Theorem still helps us in Part 4,
  because it applies to the sampling distribution of the *mean*, not to the
  raw scores.

# Part 4: Conduct a One-Sample Hypothesis Test

Test whether the class mean differs significantly from a claimed value of 60.

* H₀: μ = 60
* H₁: μ ≠ 60 (two-tailed test), with α = 0.05

```{r ttest}
t_test_result <- t.test(scores, mu = 60, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
print(t_test_result)

# Extract key values
t_statistic <- unname(t_test_result$statistic)
df_t        <- unname(t_test_result$parameter)
p_value     <- t_test_result$p.value
ci_lower    <- t_test_result$conf.int[1]
ci_upper    <- t_test_result$conf.int[2]

# Interpretation
cat("Test Statistic (t):", round(t_statistic, 3), "\n")
cat("P-value:", round(p_value, 4), "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval: [", round(ci_lower, 2), ",", round(ci_upper, 2), "]\n")
```

```{r effect-size}
# Effect size (Cohen's d) for a one-sample test
cohens_d <- (mean_score - 60) / sd_score
round(cohens_d, 3)
```

**Interpretation.** We conducted a one-sample t-test to assess whether the
class mean (`r round(mean_score, 2)`) differs significantly from the claimed
mean of 60. The t-statistic is `r round(t_statistic, 3)` on `r df_t` degrees of
freedom, with p = `r round(p_value, 4)`. At the α = 0.05 significance level, we
**reject the null hypothesis** (p < 0.05). The 95% confidence interval
[`r round(ci_lower, 2)`, `r round(ci_upper, 2)`] does not contain 60, so the
data provide evidence that the true mean is **below** 60. The effect is small,
though: Cohen's d = `r round(cohens_d, 2)`, a gap of about
`r round(60 - mean_score, 1)` marks. Because we rejected H₀, the error we could
be making is a **Type I error** (rejecting a true null; its probability is
capped at α = 0.05). A Type II error is only possible when we *fail* to reject.

**Checking the assumptions.** The t-test assumes independent observations and an
approximately normal sampling distribution of the mean. The raw scores are not
normal (Part 3), but with n = `r nrow(results)` the Central Limit Theorem makes
the test reasonably reliable. Even so, the skew matters here, so we run a
robustness check with a rank-based test of whether the *median* differs from 60.

```{r wilcoxon}
wilcox_result <- wilcox.test(scores, mu = 60, exact = FALSE)
print(wilcox_result)
```

This test gives p = `r round(wilcox_result$p.value, 3)`, which is **not**
significant, and the sample median (`r round(median_score, 2)`) is actually
above 60. The two tests answer different questions. The *mean* is below 60
because of the low-scoring tail, but the *typical* (median) student is not
below 60. So the claim "the class average is 60" is rejected for the mean, but
this should not be read as "most students scored below 60".

# Extension: Questions Beyond the Template

## Does attendance relate to the total score?

```{r attendance}
ggplot(results, aes(x = att_total, y = total_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Total score vs sessions attended",
       x = "Sessions attended (out of 20)", y = "Total Score") +
  theme_minimal()

cor_test <- cor.test(results$att_total, results$total_score)
print(cor_test)
fit <- lm(total_score ~ att_total, data = results)
coef(fit)
```

Attendance and total score are strongly positively correlated
(r = `r round(unname(cor_test$estimate), 2)`, p < 0.001). On average, each
extra session attended goes with about `r round(coef(fit)[["att_total"]], 1)`
more marks. This is an *association*, not proof of cause: attendance also
feeds directly into the score (attendance marks are part of the continuous
assessment), and motivated students tend to do both.

## What proportion of the class passes?

```{r pass-rate}
n_pass <- sum(results$pass_fail == "Pass")
binom_result <- binom.test(n_pass, nrow(results))
print(binom_result)

table(results$grade)
```

`r n_pass` of `r nrow(results)` students passed
(`r round(100 * n_pass / nrow(results), 1)`%). The exact 95% confidence
interval for the true pass rate is
[`r round(100 * binom_result$conf.int[1], 1)`%,
`r round(100 * binom_result$conf.int[2], 1)`%]. This is the binomial model from
Part 3 applied to real data.
